description.narrative: The Economic Management Capacity Building Project for Ghana aims at supporting the government to define and perform its role as a facilitator for economic development. Project components: Component 1) will support the development of a framework for prioritization, consensus building and budgeting of public sector reform objectives. Component 2) will support strengthening of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Component 3) will support strengthening of Bank of Ghana (BOG). Component 4) will support the National Insurance Commission (NIC) in (i) providing technical assistance for the design of the curriculum and strategic plan; (ii) revising and instituting a modern legal and regulatory insurance framework; (iii) capacity building to improve insurance supervision; and (iv) capacity building support to the research and actuarial units;. Component 5) will: (i) provide support to review Ghana Stock Exchange (GSE) rules and regulations; (ii) provide expertise to manage the business and regulatory risks of demutualization; (iii) support GSE automation; and (iv) build GSE staff capacity and that of market operators. Component 6) This component aims to: (i) support the strengthening of legislation for the governance of the pensions sector; (ii) evaluate and design a process for such outsourcing of SSNIT's investment management functions; (iii) strengthen the capacity of SSNIT staff to undertake actuarial simulations of revenue and benefit flows according to different medium-term reform scenarios; and (iv) strengthen the timeliness and accuracy of individual data account records. Component 7) will seek to establish a strengthened banking and non-bank financial institutions system that provides a wide range of competitive products.

The objective of the Project is to support the Recipient to perform its role as a facilitator for economic development through: (i) implementation by MDAs of a reform initiative for improved public sector management and service delivery; and (ii) strengthening of the governance and competitiveness of the financial sector

% of insurance companies inspected within the year by NIC based on agreedtemplate

comment.narrative: Given the change underway towards risk-based supervision, 100% on-site inspection rate may not now be acheived. RBS requireattention and supervisory recourses to be focused on risky companies. The requirement to inspect every company at least once intwo yearsis therefore not risk based. Moreover the previous data as provided are on 24months basis as stipulated in the NIC Acthowever, thisrequirement has been taken out of the new insurance Bill. The NIC is therefore not targeting a 100% inspection ratejust for the sake of it. Inspections are now based on risk and the need for regulatory attention. It is therefore not likely thatit will achievea 100% inspection any time soon due to the new course being taken.

title.narrative: NIC Compliance with IAIS Core Principles as determined by WB/IMF ROSC review

comment.narrative:
There are a number of projects currently in progress the completion of which is very likely to improve significantly compliancewith the IAIS Core Principles. They are the (i) the Legal review, (ii) Implementation of Risk Based Supervision, (iii)Implementation of IFRS by the insurance companies, (iv) submission of electronic returns by the insurance companies to the NIC and(v) the development of a risk based solvency framework. This means that the projects benefits of significantly lifting thecompliance level would be achieved fully by 2013/2014.
The ICPs were reviewed by the IAIS at its October 2011 meeting in Seoul,Korea. The review has significantly changed the dynamics, contents and requirements of the ICPs. For example, before the review,the ICPs were just about 50 pages. Now they are about 500 pages. Again, following the recent financial crises, some of therequirements are now stricter than before.

BOG Compliance with relevant Basel Core Principles

comment.narrative:
Complaint 1 largely complaint 13 Materially complaint 8 Non compliant 3 (using the 2006 methodology). At the start of the projectthe Basel principles were assessed based on the 1999 Core Principles Methodology by Reports on the Observance of Standards andCodes (ROSC) in 2006 which gave the Bank of Ghana a compliance level of 80% and by the end of 2009 the Bank of Ghana had achievedfull compliance based on the recommendations of ROSC. Thus if this report should be based on the benchmark indicator that prevailedin the 1999 Core Principles then the Bank of Ghana is 100% compliance for the period 2010-2012 as well.
However, in 2006 theBasel Committee issued a significantly improved version of the Core Principles Methodology on which the Bank of Ghana was assessedby the IMF andthe World Bank as contained in the 2010 FSAP report. Based on this new methodology, the Bank was compliant with 1principle, largelycompliant with 13 principles, materially non-compliant with 8 principles and non-compliant with 3 principles.
This means overall the compliance level has reduced to about 50% since most of the principles have been merged and new onesintroduced. In addition, theassessment criteria have been changed in terms of the definitions and classification from fullycompliant, largely compliant andnotrelevant to those outlined below:
Compliant A country is considered compliant with aPrinciple when all essential criteriaapplicable for this country are met without any significant deficiencies.
Largelycompliant A country is considered largely compliant with a Principle whenever only minor shortcomings are observed which do notraise any concerns about the authoritys ability andclear intent to achieve full compliance with the Principle within a prescribedperiod of time.
Materially non-compliant A country is considered materially non-compliant with a Principle whenever there aresevere shortcomings, despite the existence of formalrules, regulations and procedures, and there is evidence that supervision hasclearly not been effective, that practical implementationis weak, or that the shortcomings are sufficient to raise doubts about theauthoritys ability to achieve compliance.
Non-compliant A country is considered non-compliant with a Principle whenever therehas been no substantive implementation of the Principle,several essential criteria are not complied with or supervision ismanifestly ineffective.
